title: From Brahma to Shaunaka
hookLine: who taught your teacher's teacher? an Upanishad names the chain, and a letter of Paul's looks ahead
carry: parampara: the teaching passes hand to hand
tomorrow: why would an Upanishad stop to list its teachers' names?

cards: Ask someone who taught them a family recipe and the answer starts running backward. My aunt. Well, she got it from her mother-in-law.
Who got it from a neighbor back home, maybe. Every skill you have came through a chain of hands. So: who taught your teacher's teacher?
The Mundaka Upanishad opens by answering that question for itself.

teach.b: Its first lines name a lineage. Brahma, first of the gods, maker of all, taught the knowledge of Brahman to Atharvan, his eldest son. Atharvan told it to Angir.
Angir to Satyavaha, of the Bharadvaja family. He handed it to Angiras.
Then a householder named Shaunaka comes to Angiras, the right way, and asks: what is it that, once known, makes all this known? The chain exists so that question can be asked.

Hindus call this parampara, the unbroken line from teacher to student, and it's why many Hindu teachers still say whose student they are before they teach. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words.

In the New Testament, Paul writes to a younger man, Timothy: "the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also."
The same letter remembers the faith that lived first in Timothy's grandmother Lois. Shared: a teaching passes person to person, and the passing is part of the teaching. And an honest difference.
The Mundaka names its chain backward, all the way up to Brahma, and the knowledge is of Brahman. Paul's chain runs forward to people not yet named, and what's handed on is the message about Jesus.
One looks up the line; one looks down it. Both put a person at each link.

how: In some Hindu schools students learn the names of their line of teachers and recite them before study; the Mundaka Upanishad itself opens with such a line.

o: a teaching handed from one person to the next
a family tree of kings, written on a palace wall
a list of rules copied from an older book

games.q: who handed it to whom. tap the pairs.
p: came to Angiras with a question
commit it to those who'll teach others

s: the Mundaka's chain begins with a human teacher
it begins with Brahma, first of the gods, maker of all.
Paul's letter asks Timothy to hand on what he heard to people who will teach others
2 Timothy 2:2: 'faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.'
the two chains hand on the same teaching in different words
both pass it person to person; what's handed on differs: knowledge of Brahman, and the message about Jesus.

games.q: Shaunaka reaches the end of the chain and stands before Angiras. what does he ask?
o: who taught you, and who taught them?
what is it that, once known, makes all this known?
how soon can I become a teacher?
games.why: Mundaka 1.1.3: the chain exists so the big question can be asked. the rest of the Upanishad answers it.

practice: Say aloud, softly, the name of one person who taught you something you still use. Then, if you know it, the name of the person who taught them. Let each name sit in the air for a breath before the next.

wordCard.voice: A lineage: a teaching passed person to person, what Hindus call parampara. The Mundaka names its chain back to Brahma; a letter of Paul's hands it forward.

orig.note: Sanskrit: knowledge of Brahman, what the Mundaka's chain hands down.

carryVoice: Keep this: parampara, the teaching passes hand to hand. Every link in it has a name, even the ones we've forgotten.

sources.ref: Mundaka Upanishad 1.1.1–1.1.3 (Brahma, first of the gods, maker of all, protector of the world, told the knowledge of Brahman to Atharvan, his eldest son; Atharvan to Angir; Angir to Satyavaha Bharadvaja; he to Angiras; Shaunaka, a great householder, approached Angiras duly and asked: what is that which being known, all this becomes known?)
